Nevertheless, training DNNs is notoriously time-consuming and requires significant computational resources. To address this challenge, researchers have successfully applied the block coordinate descent (BCD) algorithm to linear models by splitting DNN training into smaller linear sub-problems. These models leverage the uniqueness of natural images, as confirmed by several image priors such as BM3D and ANLA, to achieve impressive results. Building upon this work, we introduce a new algorithm called block coordinate descent with alternating non-convex minimization (BCD-ANCM) that utilizes three-dimensional image patches to solve each linear sub-problem efficiently. Notably, BCD-ANCM achieves this without the need for sophisticated data augmentation, acceleration algorithms or the employment of external priors.

This work takes this understanding a step further by exploring the fundamental characteristics of linear and nonlinear transformations that make small neural networks perform so well. Unfortunately, this advancement has created an opportunity for medical information to be compromised. A notable threat in this context is the development of sophisticated attacks involving data transfer from one healthcare setting to another. Presently, there is a notable lack of research into anomalous EHR transactions, specifically focusing on transfers between separate entities within the healthcare system. A notable shortage exists in regards to established benchmarks and comprehensive evaluation frameworks for detecting such anomalies. In order to bridge this gap, this study establishes two new datasets consisting of real-world EHR anomalies derived from publicly available sources, along with a comprehensive benchmark that incorporates multiple classification techniques for comparing the performance of different machine learning models in detecting these anomalies. A notable advantage of this benchmark lies in its flexibility to accommodate diverse healthcare settings based on transaction flow patterns, thereby providing a holistic framework for evaluating and pinpointing the most difficult-to-detect anomalies within EHRs.

one-body, strong interaction studies for few-body systems consisting of nucleons, specifically with protons being the subject. This program is called PROSIT, short for PROton SCattering for Internal Structure and Threshold issues. It is built on top of the SCET approach, taking into consideration relativistic wave functions and their implications on threshold enhancement and shape functions. Additionally, PROSIT includes the effects of target nucleon polarizability and relativistic corrections to its spin. Two-body interactions are represented by dispersion relations incorporating experimental data and monopole interactions to ensure stability of the bound systems. Moreover, PROSIT allows for threshold expansion and relativistic charge and magnetic form factors calculations at any energy. It is notable that these features are uncommon in general purpose few-body calculation codes. Furthermore, PROSIT has been validated by comparing its results to established approaches and experiments, showing excellent correspondence.

outcomes for 54 galaxies that underwent $^{12}$C$^{16}$O and $^{13}$C$^{16}$O spectroscopic assessments using the 50m radio telescope. Our observations focused on molecular gas rotations within the central 10 kiloparsecs of each galaxy, yielding nearly complete maps of CO emission. The data were collected over seven to fifteen hours of integrated exposure time, with a minimum of 2000 seconds, across various antenna configurations from 2 to 12 baselines. Our final processed data set is composed of 476 baseline-hours of signal-to-noise ratio 3 and above. Notably, CO emission above this threshold is present in 88% of the mapped areas; in regions below this threshold, the CO emission averages 0.05 times the average of regions above the threshold. We provide one-dimensional spectra for 705 baseline-hours of data that did not meet the signal-to-noise requirement along with 21 isolated CO emission lines from 54 galaxies. Additionally, we present 13 new minor mergers candidates identified through CO mapping along with updated merger classifications for 29 galaxies previously recognized as major or minor mergers. Our analysis highlights the value of mapping internal gas rotations to assess galaxy rotation curves and ponders the relationship between angular momentum conservation during minor mergers and the resulting rotation curve effects.

This can be achieved by reducing photographic star field weak lensing errors in galaxy surveys to less than 0.3 percent efficiency. To accomplish this at the Kilo-Degree Survey's scale, it is necessary to develop new, highly efficient methods for analyzing the shear measurements of multiple stars in a single image of the sky. This study introduces an entirely new technique, based on optimal estimation theory, that applies the most efficient possible methods to process the shear measurements of all the stars in an image simultaneously. By running extensive simulations of the Kilo-Degree Survey and analyzing the results with this new method, it is shown that the star field weak lensing errors can be reduced to less than 0.3 percent efficiency as required. The most significant limitations of the method, however, remain the stars' instrumental bias and the shear measurements' variance, which are introduced by the process itself and exceed the baseline values by up to three and four orders of magnitude, respectively. Nevertheless, the new method demonstrates superior performance to the conventional baseline method for processing individual stars, offering a key advantage in preparing surveys for the next generation of galaxy surveys such as LSST.

C) simulations are a vital tool for statistical inference in complex models, yet their outcome is only as reliable as the MCMC sampling method employed. This study focuses on analyzing the sampling efficiency of common MCMC techniques, including the independent Metropolis-Hastings, random walk Metropolis, and uninformative Metropolis algorithms, for modeling a latent factor representation learning model. The investigator examined various factors that affect sampling time, including the number of MCMC iterations, factor representation dimensionality, and data distributional skewness. A formal measure of MCMC convergence rate was proposed and utilized in a thorough comparison of the sampling efficiency of the mentioned MCMC methods. The results reveal that the standard Metropolis algorithm exhibits optimal sampling efficiency in this study, and the implications of these findings for modeling stock returns and evaluating the performance of portfolio managers are presented.

operator is analyzed in its most general form in a curved spacetime setting. A specific type of gravitational field, represented by the Godel universe, is used as the backdrop for this examination. This universe possesses a static and spherically symmetric metric that enables the reduction of the Dirac operator to a set of separable Schrodinger-like equations. An alternative approach to the Dirac operator in a curved spacetime is also explored, resulting in the creation of a potential energy function that is derivable from the electromagnetic vector potential. A solution to the Dirac equation under these conditions is proposed and it is demonstrated that this solution shares a significant overlap with the de Sitter universe. A mathematical model of a static and spherically symmetric gravitational field, characterized by the Godel universe, forms the basis of this investigation. When the electromagnetic vector potential is accounted for, a new effective potential energy arises, leading to a divergence in the wave function at a specific radius. However, when the spacetime metric undergoes a transformation to conform to the de Sitter universe, the wave function's divergence is mitigated, indicating that the universe's stability is preserved in the presence of the electromagnetic vector potential.

This study focuses on the optics of a quantum well with positively charged barriers subjected to a linearly polarized laser. These calculations are crucial for minimizing experimental uncertainties in the search for Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs). WIMP-rejection capabilities are directly correlated with the efficiency of detecting scintillation and absorption signals from nuclear recoils of the same intensity. In order to maximize this efficiency, it is essential to calibrate the thresholds of these detectors through the analysis of alpha decay from $^{222}$Rn in the experimental environment. In this paper, we present a method for accurately determining the thresholds based on the continuous nature of the scintillation and absorption signals, as well as their probabilities of occurring spontaneously. We demonstrate that this approach outperforms previous methods by providing more precise and reliable results for the detection efficiency of scintillating detectors.

distribution (PM-QKD) protocol has sparked interest regarding its security enhancements, particularly in scenarios where weak laser signals from users are redirected to a conversion device controlled by the attacker. In our research, we address the security concerns of the PM-QKD protocol by developing an all-optical conversion device that converts incoming signals from users into a single strong signal, thus overcoming potential weaknesses associated with the conversion device. However, this improvement introduces a new issue, as the conversion device could selectively convert strong signals from users with strong laser signals, thus threatening the security of the PM-QKD system. To overcome this challenge, we introduce the concept of sharing weak laser signals among multiple users, thereby enabling the security of the PM-QKD system to be guaranteed by users with strong laser signals, without incurring significant costs associated with the conversion device. Furthermore, we analyze the gain of the conversion device attack model under the proposed technique and derive the gain bound in terms of the gain of the conversion device, demonstrating that users with strong laser signals can guarantee the security of the PM-QKD system with their individual channel gain values being key factors.

To capitalize on this ability, we have developed a novel technique for generating new text by modifying existing text. This technique, called T5-Edit, views text generation as a series of iterative edits performed on initial context. Despite the theoretical limitations imposed by the Koehler-Porter law, which stipulates that a job's processing time cannot depend on more than one past production decision or job dependency, we will broaden the understanding of this law to accommodate multiple past dependencies and serial-parallel job dependencies in our approach. Our algorithm utilizes a limited look-back approach to efficiently handle an extensive variety of DJSP scenarios, including those with independent, dependent, cumulative, step, polynomial, exponential, and randomly generated processing times. Our experiments demonstrate our method's capability to provide optimal solutions across a wide range of DJSP scenarios.

O3 ceramics indicate the presence of unusual, long-range, anisotropic transport phenomena linked to a non-degenerate electronic state at the Fermi level.  In order to explore the underlying causes of these observed transport properties and how they are connected, we first identify a specific, low-temperature regime characterized by localized, near-Fermi-level state that is disentangled from the superconducting phase.  We then establish a theoretical framework that bridges the localized, disconnected Fermi-level state with the more complex, possibly superconducting state found at higher temperatures.  This framework is utilized to create a general, quantitative model that reproduces the precise, experimentally-measured values of the normalized, low-temperature resistivity and the associated, non-linear Hall voltage.  Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the more complex, possibly superconducting state shares fundamental characteristics with the phase known as the unusual iron-based superconducting state, and that the near-Fermi-level state that is disentangled from the superconducting phase could be realized through the introduction of specific, localized structural or chemical disorders.

Despite their successive deployments in high-stakes fields such as healthcare and transportation, the underlying workings of these models remain poorly understood. Existing explanations such as salience and feature maps only provide a shallow insight into how these models operate. In contrast, our proposed approach employs a pair of computationally efficient methods to concurrently estimate the communication costs and inference time of deep neural networks, with the ultimate goal of pinpointing the optimal model dimensions. In this research, our K-Evo algorithm is capable of identifying the subtle connections between multiple related functions, such as models sharing the same dataset but with varying hyperparameters. When a backdoor is introduced into one of these functions, our algorithm detects the interdependent hidden connections among them and eradicates the backdoor entirely. halo dark matter spike
  measurements have become highly desired in theoretical contexts. While most
  studies focus on the spike's density profile, we decide to investigate the
  cross-section impact on a dark matter particle's evolution within the halo.
  Assuming a cross-section interaction between halo and disk components, we
  developed a two-component halo model that reflects the density profile of
  the Fermi galaxy halo. Through this model, we observed the disk halo
  interaction to be insignificant when comparing the halo's inner and outer
  regions. As a result, we expect the disk-halo interaction to have a
  nonlinear effect on the halo's inner regions over its outer regions.

  $\frac{1}{r^2}$ distribution would result in a two-fold increase in the
  halo's inner mass content, when compared to its outer content. This internal
  mass accumulation enhances the formation of a dark matter spike within the
  halo's center. As for the disk-halo interaction's nonlinear effect, we found
  it to result in a more pronounced spike. Therefore, we suggest that a
  detailed knowledge of a galaxy's internal mass content is necessary in

To effectively exert influence, it is crucial to understand the causal structures underlying the agents' decisions. on Alfv\'en wave propagation in a barotropic plasma, characterized by a linear temperature profile and varying density, has been examined in a confined environment.  The analysis was conducted using a semi-linear MHD model, which accounted for the variation in resistivity across the plasma.  Results showing the impact of a non-uniform magnetic field were obtained numerically and are presented alongside solutions from a linearized approach.  A key finding indicates that Alfv\'en wave behavior changes when the magnetic field strength varies significantly, exhibiting either a localized or distant return to the original wave pattern, depending on the specific conditions. for a linear differential game, where the dynamics are governed by a linear time-invariant system with distinct optimal control objectives. The notable aspect of this system lies in its non-differentiable switching behavior caused by simultaneous application of maximal control efforts by competing players. Our primary objective is to develop a model that can learn from historical data and accurately predict future system states. Although the system is deterministic, its unpredictable nature arises from the unavoidable fluctuations in data generated by the stochastic control policies used to train it. The problem is compounded by the simultaneous application of maximal control efforts by competing players, resulting in an impossible to invert system matrix. To overcome this challenge, we refine the system by only utilizing data generated by the oldest successful attacks, effectively eliminating the impossible to invert matrix issue. In the absence of this problem, we would typically demand the impossibility of directly influencing another player's dynamics. Under these conditions, we establish the existence of an optimal predictive control policy that minimizes expected costs, and demonstrate its effectiveness using both simulation and laboratory tests.

binary black hole mergers in scalar tidal disruption scenarios have been studied in a theoretical context. However, for high-mass ratio cases, further research is needed to fully understand the impact of spin due to limited simulated data. As part of the preparation, it is crucial to study how the combination of these observations and the mission's anticipated outcomes will affect its own results. This combination, which accounts for the satellite's intrinsics and the characteristics of the sky it is observing, has been mathematically modeled through a realistic simulation of the data processed by the four optical channels. This processing includes removing the satellite's own contributions, deblending sources that are close together, and applying noise reduction techniques. Once the data was processed in this manner, it was analyzed to determine how it would affect the measurable properties of the sources observed by Euclid, specifically their colors. These simulations revealed that there will be a bias in the color measurements due to the saturation of the detectors' responses under low-light conditions. This bottleneck created by the satellites' intrinsics will likely impact the mission's ongoing research and its ultimate conclusions about the universe.

  the calculation of forces and potential energies precisely. However, the 
  restriction of using discrete samples to approximate averages leads to a noise 
  problem, especially when accouting for thermal fluctuations. We resolve this 
  issue by deriving a set of stochastic Hamiltonian differential equations that 
  directly yield the desired thermal fluctuations of forces and other thermodynamic 
  quantities, without the need for subsequent applications of the ergodic theorem. 
  This method can be combined with the Monte Carlo with multiple targets technique 
  to accurately obtain results for thermal fluctuations. We demonstrate the 
  benefits of this approach by comparing our results to the exact statistical 
  properties derived from the power spectrum of the forces experienced by a harmonic 
  oscillator in thermal equilibrium.

Despite their financial significance, previous research has overlooked the time complexity of transactions between smart contracts.  In this study, we analyzed the transaction graph of Ethereum smart contracts and discovered a distinguishing characteristic - transactions between contracts that have not previously interacted take significantly longer to process.  We attribute this disparity to the diverse processing times of individual transactions and propose an intuitive explanation rooted in how Ethereum processes transactions in batches.  To confirm our findings, we developed and tested several theories using statistical analysis and data visualization.  Our research revealed that, despite the inherent variability in transaction processing times, there are distinct patterns in processing times for different types of transactions.  In fact, our data shows that transactions falling within certain time ranges are associated with delayed processing and that this phenomenon is consistent across different Ethereum hard forks.  We have publicly shared our code and data to facilitate further research in this area.

Despite extensive research, some crucial aspects of GRBs remain poorly understood, especially those related to their magnetic properties. To address this knowledge gap, we have investigated a sample of 1000 energetic long-duration GRBs using far infrared and submillimeter data from Herschel-SPIRE, in combination with historical observations of these events. Our analysis reveals that dusty long-duration GRBs tend to occur at lower redshifts, which could be the result of their progenitor stars being more likely to occur in more nearby star-forming galaxies with higher dust content. Interestingly, their magnetic field strength appears to remain unaffected by the presence of dust.

embedding field asks for the maximum number of regions an embedding of a given planar graph will have, given a specific rotation scheme at the graph's edges. This question was answered by Euler, who stated that the number of regions would be one more than half the number of edges in the graph. This note delves into modifications of this question, where specific types of angles are required between adjacent edge rotations, resulting in new graphs formed through periodic planar embeddings. It is shown that if all inner angles between rotations are at least 180 degrees, the new graph is essentially double the original graph without any overlapping edges, and can be constructed using any method of embedding the original graph. If angles are 120 degrees or less, the new graph has a regional count proportional to $(\frac{1}{2}d)^2$, where $d$ is the number of edges in the original graph, indicating a significant increase in regions for smaller angles.

In this context, it's crucial to assess the reliability of these models in anticipating and avoiding unexpected obstacles in complex scenarios. A common approach to achieve this is by using robustness tests to evaluate how well a trained model performs under normal conditions. However, due to practical limitations, testing every possible scenario is impractical. Instead, we need to identify more critical test cases that can help us gauge a model's robustness and overall safety in real-world situations. In this research, we've developed a method to pinpoint these decisive test cases by leveraging intermediate network features and their spatial information. Our findings demonstrate that models performing well on these identified high-benefit test cases are more likely to exhibit robust performance in general. We've also established a strong correlation between robust performance and the spatial distribution of features at specific layers in the network. Ultimately, our approach can assist in streamlining the process of robust model development by pinpointing crucial cases that lead to general robustness.

independent imaginary part of the gluon self-energy in SU(N) Yang-Mills theory for any number of spacetime dimensions greater than or equal to four, expressed in terms of the renormalization group function $\rho$ that influences the gluon propagator. The self-energy's imaginary component was initially determined by Novikov, Shirkov, and Teryaev for four-dimensional space and by Sobreira and Perezak for a range of five-dimensional spaces. Understanding how these fractures affect seismic wave speed and conductivity is essential for interpreting seismic data in mining and volcanic settings.  Previous studies have measured the effect of fractures on seismic wave speed and conductivity using a variety of measurements, including dip and strike angles, but have not considered their impact on uncertainty.  In this research, a new approach is presented that utilizes a global optimization method to account for uncertainty in model parameters, resulting in enhanced models of wave speed and conductivity.  This method is applied to real-world data from the Mount Eden gold mine and Campi Flegrei caldera, yielding improved models of wave speed and conductivity, as well as a metric of model uncertainty.  The findings suggest that large uncertainties in model parameters can produce distinct patterns in wave speed and conductivity, particularly related to fracture orientation and distribution, and that these patterns can provide valuable information for enhancing the interpretation of seismic data in mining and volcanic settings.

This inquiry applies to monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides with spin-polarized electrons and graphene on a Wuornos-Style substrate of spin-polarized materials, all of which exhibit similar behavior. Our analysis combines renormalization group methods and numerical observations to demonstrate that the coupling terms consistently follow a specific power-law relationship with energy, specifically proportional to $(\Lambda/W)^2$, where $\Lambda$ represents the energy range and $W$ signifies the width of that range. A unified theoretical framework has yet to be developed to comprehensively explain these phenomena and their observed characteristics.  A key obstacle in constructing such a framework is the lack of numerical codes enabling in-depth, resolved radio-source simulations necessary for accurately modeling FXTs.  In this paper, a set of simplified, general-purpose codes have been developed from first principles, using either relativistic electron-inertial radiation reactions or particle collisions as the interaction model.  These new codes, along with existing ones, have been incorporated into a unified, multi-code ensemble framework that employs an ensemble-based method to achieve coherent output.  This code ensemble, comprising six different (MHD, relativistic electron, particle, and two single-fluid) models, has been utilized to simulate a notable FXT candidate - an explosive interaction between a narrow radio jet and a dense gas ring surrounding a massive radio galaxy.  Through a set of proxy variables representing both electron and particle fluid quantities, the ensemble was able to explore a wide parameter space and produce a range of possible outcomes from its simulations, ultimately providing insights that could aid in future observational efforts.

neural networks can resist deception when trained with malicious data.  A common hypothesis posits that this is because these models spread their mass across many weak connections, making them resistant to manipulation.  However, our research indicates that this hypothesis may be inaccurately simplified.  By simulating real-world training environments, we discovered that the resistance to deception observed in practice is actually a by-product of how these models organize their parameters in relation to each other.  Specifically, healthy models differ significantly from unhealthy ones in terms of the unique combinations of parameters they use to process input data.  This distinction holds true regardless of how we measure it - whether it's by looking at the entire network at once or focusing on individual layers.  Our research also shows that incorporating an alternative optimization method known as the quasi-Newton method can produce models that are not only more accurate but also more resistant to deception.  By incorporating an explicit constraint to restrict the number of new parameters introduced during training, we can achieve even greater resistance.  When tested against each other, these methods demonstrated a significant difference in how resistant they were to deception - with one approach yielding a 10 times greater resistance than the other.  When compared to each other, models that are both more accurate and more resistant to deception are uniquely characterized by how they organize their parameters in relation to each other - providing concrete guidelines that can be used to design new optimization algorithms.  These methods have the potential to be of great value in the future development of neural networks

A novel communication framework, the concurrent read/write model, was introduced to address this need, aiming to optimize performance through parallel data transfers and synchronized data access.  Although promising, this approach has not been extensively explored in practical applications.  To bridge this gap, we develop a concurrent read/write protocol, titled CR-WP, tailored for star-structured mega satellite networks.  By allocating specific data transmission slots and enabling simultaneous data transfers, our protocol enhances network efficiency and reduces latency.  In theoretical performances, our approach outdoes conventional TCP/IP protocols, and through a collaborative effort with satellite industry experts, we refined the protocol by adapting it to networks with variable data transfer rates.  Experimental results validate the enhanced protocol, yielding superior outcomes compared to industry standards.  Our innovative protocol has the potential to revolutionize high-speed satellite communication protocols and provide valuable insights for further concurrent read/write protocol development.

  the time-harmonic acoustic pressure equation to include an obstacle with a smooth,

  the Nystr\"{o}m method. This involves transforming the differential equation into

a Euclidean space's boundary determines a linear order on its orderable groups.  For spaces with more than one component, however, this orderable group property has remained an open question.  We answer this question by showing that the boundary of a two-component Euclidean space with a planar boundary has a linear order, thereby implying the same for all Euclidean spaces with a surface boundary.  To do this, we establish a broader result: any orderable group that can be embedded in a boundary group from a Euclidean space with a surface boundary also has a group orderable by left translations, a property equivalent to being orderable by permutations.  From this, we derive the specific consequence that the boundary of a two-component Euclidean space is orderable by left translations.

of semi-Supervised learning over supervised learning has long been a fascinating yet challenging problem. Recent research suggests this phenomenon can be explained by a novel framework that leverages frustration-based theory. This approach proposes that the disparity arises from the specific type of data used in each learning method, which creates distinct epistemic states with inherent contradictions, thereby generalizing more effectively. Nevertheless, if the data does not contain these fractal patterns, the proposed framework's advantage over supervised learning methods disappears. To test this theory, we developed a simple model that replicates the observed semi-supervised learning advantage in a theoretical framework known as the "Fraternal Generalization Effect" (FGE. To validate FGE across diverse settings, we designed an experimental framework that incorporates various model types, dataset combinations, and learning algorithms. Our results confidently support the FGE hypothesis, indicating that semi-supervised learning's generalization improvement can be attributed to its ability to learn from complex, self-similar data patterns that are particularly effective at generalizing.

While discrete topological features, such as connections between nodes, provide valuable information, continuous characteristics, like curvature and surface area, offer even more insightful measures of a network's complex architecture. However, obtaining accurate estimates of these quantities is challenging due to the need for dense sampling points within the network's underlying space. We present a statistical topology framework that enables the extraction of intrinsic geometric information from a network by utilizing its functional output values, effectively capturing higher-order properties and providing a more comprehensive understanding of the network's topological structure. Through the use of Bessel kernels and the integration of network data, we derive precise formulas for computing various geometric and topological quantities, including Euler characteristic, Gauss-Bonnet sum, and Begleman-Dowker-Chern classes. Our method is demonstrated with financial network examples based on European option prices and gravitational waves, showing significant advantages over existing techniques that rely solely on dense grid sampling.

Our approach focuses on creating a control policy that ensures compliance with hard constraints on system states resulting from various input actions. We establish a precise theoretical framework within which our approach is valid, and our results are applicable to a broad category of systems characterized by inputs with distinct effects, such as those with inputs behaving as saturated linear systems, Morse-Fleming systems, and others. Our key contribution involves formulating a optimization problem that yields a critically safe control policy, and we demonstrate its computational feasibility through an efficient algorithm called Projected Sliding Surface Optimization (PSO). We showcase the effectiveness of our method by developing and testing a critically safe controller for an actual nonlinear aircraft control system.

In this research, we explore how diverse network graphs behave around this epidemic threshold. a pressing issue for security and law enforcement agencies, who need to rapidly identify key individuals in high-stakes situations such as active shooter scenarios.  While AI-powered object detection technology has made significant progress in recent years, applying it to real-world settings presents a challenge due to issues like false positives, low precision predictions, and the need for manual verification.  In an effort to address these problems, research has been conducted into automatic association of detected individuals with their actual identities, based on the location and context of the detected bounding boxes.  While this approach has shown some promise, it has not yet been tested at a large enough scale to provide a truly comprehensive understanding of its effectiveness.  To facilitate larger-scale experiments, a new dataset has been created called Real-World Shooter Association (RWSA), which features a specialized task known as shooter association.  This dataset, constructed from over 500 pages of police reports and featuring a total of 10,000 manually annotated images, is unique in that it involves multiple challenges simultaneously, including individual identification, where the task requires labeling the bounding boxes of detected shooters regardless of whether they are fully visible, partially visible, or occulted by other objects.  A thorough analysis has been conducted of the current state-of-the-art vision models in relation to the RWSA dataset, which showed a significant gap in terms of accuracy, particularly in terms of false positives, low precision predictions, and the need for manual verification that is so prevalent in real-world applications.

in cancer image classification, a critical issue persists - understanding their decision-making processes. Research into explaining the predictions of these models has yielded approaches like salient score learning, which focuses on identifying key features associated with the diagnosis. However, these approaches have certain limitations, particularly in cases where the underlying image patterns are complex and diverse. To address this, we propose a novel framework called Dual-Path Residual Mixtures (DPRM) for explaining predictions in super-resolution cancer image classification tasks. This framework leverages two separate feature learning pathways - one focused on low-resolution images and another on high-resolution images - to extract respective feature matrices. Building upon the Dual-Path Residual Mixtures, we develop a comprehensive method called Dual-Path Residual Mixtures for Classification (DPRMC). This method combines the two feature matrices through progressive mixture layers, allowing for the generation of mix-feature maps associated with the diagnosis. Furthermore, we define a calculation mechanism called calculation mixture layer (CML) to compute mix-feature maps from mix-score maps derived from two separate score maps, thereby producing output classifications. The experimental evaluations of our proposed approach, conducted in relation to the LIDC-IDRI dataset and CAMM dataset for cancer image super-resolution and classification respectively, demonstrate its superiority over existing alternatives.

model to explain massive Dirac eigenvalue spectra in a range of $k$ values, particularly those associated with a topological insulator's surface states. The model incorporates a minimal number of assumptions about the interplay between a strong uniform electric field and the surface states' rapid dispersion in different directions. Under a uniform electric field, the model's band structure exhibits a non-trivial surface state with the desired eigenvalue pattern, thus providing a clear mechanism for understanding Z$_2$ trivial or non-trivial surface state patterns associated with the desired eigenvalue spectra. The model also predicts emergent Lorentz symmetry near certain high-symmetry $k$ points, allowing us to derive a nearly free fermion model that includes interaction terms. Theoretical predictions about the model's behavior under strain, chemical doping, and other perturbations that break Lorentz invariance are also presented. The model's surface physics can be verified by various experimental methods, such as angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), which shows the non-trivial surface state in question.

For any given configuration, the dynamics is defined by transitioning from the current state to a new state based on the state of neighboring sites, with specific rules depending on the occupation of nearby sites.  The goal of this work is to analyze the exclusion process when sites follow an infinite-range dynamic, where the decision to change the state of a site is solely based on the overall charge within a particular radius.  It has been demonstrated that this model maintains duality properties and undergoes a phase transition from irreversibility to reversibility at a certain temperature.  Additionally, it was found that the nonequilibrium stationary state can be expressed in terms of equilibrated, charge-carrying exclusions processes.  Furthermore, a nonequilibrium version of the Uhlenbeck transport coefficient was successfully measured and found to be in line with predictions based on a different method of calculation.

Hatcher independently developed an approach to framing smooth hypersurfaces within Euclidean space, building upon earlier work by Porter. This paper extends their findings to include the case of hypersurfaces with edges, effectively adapting the framing concept to a higher-dimensional context. An auxiliary surface is introduced and demonstrated to be equivalent to the original framing objective, thereby expanding the framework's applicability. Additionally, the paper shows that, much like smooth hypersurfaces, frames of hypersurfaces with edges are uniquely determined up to a certain class of deformations.

The immobilized polymers are initially randomly dispersed and interact with each other and the mobile polymer through a suitable potential. The model we analyze includes relevant interactions such as hard cores, electrostatic forces, and van der Waals forces. The study focuses on the distribution of end-to-end distances of the mobile polymer as it navigates through the frozen landscape, which we calculate using the method of functional renewal. The result yields a non-universal discrete lobe-like structure surrounding the mobile polymer's starting position, as well as a universal exponential decay pattern of the end-to-end distance probability distribution, similar to the model of Taylor and Weisinger.

significant progress in studying
  quantum many-body systems through simulations, which has led to multiple key
  breakthroughs. While classical Monte Carlo methods have been a reliable tool
  for this purpose, the realisation of experimental quantum simulation and the
  growing influence of quantum computing have sparked renewed interest in
  computational quantum many-body theory. This interest is driven by the
  potential to use digital quantum computers to surpass the limitations of
  classical simulations and observe distinctive quantum phenomena exceeding
  classical expectations. This potential has sparked multiple proposals to
  employ digital quantum processors in simulations, which has resulted in
  ongoing debates about the most effective algorithms, strategies for error
  reduction, and the practicality of achieving realistic simulations. This
  review aims to provide an overview of theoretical developments in computational
  quantum many-body theory from a digital perspective, encompassing new
  quantum algorithms, enhancements of error tolerance, and the integration of
  artificial intelligence and machine learning.

characterized by bronchiectasis, results from chronic inflammation leading to recurring obstructive bronchial infections. This condition triggers a cyclic progression of injury to airway walls, comprised of bronchial inflammation, damage, and scarring, ultimately leading to dilatation and fibrosis. Advances in computational power and machine learning have made it possible to model the structural and functional changes in bronchiectatic airways using patient-specific CT scans, potentially leading to advancements in diagnosis, treatment monitoring, and development of targeted treatment tools. This study introduces a method to automatically segment and characterize the morphology of airway walls in CT scans using deep learning techniques. Following this, a finite element simulation is used to model the mechanical properties of airway walls, incorporating the effects of weight, stiffness, and viscosity. This airway wall model can be applied to guide minimally invasive diagnostic and therapeutic interventions, such as bronchoscopy, electrophysiology, and gene therapy, allowing for more accurate procedure planning and boosting their effectiveness.

specific source: binary black hole mergers taking place in the early universe, specifically during the inflationary era. Since the vast majority of these mergers will result in undetectable signals by current gravitational wave detectors, we examine an alternative approach using a model of inflation-derived cosmological perturbations where large-scale fluctuations give rise to significant gravitational wave production in the far universe. This model enables the prediction of a remarkably high merger rate for binary black hole events, potentially exceeding existing astrophysical estimates by several orders of magnitude. We demonstrate that even with very basic assumptions regarding black hole mass functions, a profound pattern in the gravitational wave data will emerge, namely an excessively high merger rate density observed across various black hole mass combinations. To verify or refute these theories, we outline three creative methods to reconcile theoretical predictions with observational evidence using the entire LIGO dataset.
